statements.text: Three years ago, we had a chance to get ahead of this issue. In 2024, when I chaired the Senate Commerce Committee, we passed the Future of AI Innovation Act, which would have given the federal government the ability to work with industry to independently test most advanced AI systems for serious national security risks.
statements.venue: Senate floor speech on AI risks

statements.text: If we passed these bills we would be more ahead of the game than we are today. Instead, we’ve lost three years. The technology keeps advancing. The risks keep growing and now the very dangers we’ve warned about — autonomous cyberattacks and biological weapons — are no longer theoretical. It is time that we act and act aggressively.
statements.venue: Senate floor speech on AI risks

statements.text: We must keep in mind that these AI models consistently lag about only seven months and the most powerful open models continue to come from China. So, it is time for my colleagues to come together to act.
statements.venue: Senate floor speech on AI risks

statements.text: We know that these threats are real. Cybersecurity, misinformation, building on these AI agents that could be used in military applications, we need our colleagues to say, ‘Stop with saying the industry can do what it wants’ and let’s put together the infrastructure at the federal level that not only has strong federal standards, but also has independent testing and real safeguards for the American people.
statements.venue: Senate floor speech on AI risks

statements.text: So how do we get both NIST and DOE working together on these tool assessments in determining what are true risk assessment, so they are identified, and what do we need to do to help build a workforce, particularly in skilling the workforce for AI?
statements.context: Opening statement and question at a Senate Commerce Committee hearing on AI and the Department of Energy's role in U.S. competitiveness and security.

statements.text: The U.S. Department of Justice has stated: ``Hostile foreign powers are weaponizing bulk data and the power of artificial intelligence to target Americans.'' I do not want technology in the United States used this way.
statements.context: Senate floor speech during debate on the National Security Act supplemental package, covering Ukraine, Israel, Indo-Pacific allies, sanctions, and technology policy.

statements.text: The emerging tech jobs of tomorrow are here today. Demand for AI expertise is already high and will continue to grow. This bill will open doors to AI for students at all levels, and upskill our workforce to drive American tech innovation, entrepreneurship, and progress in solving the toughest global challenges.

The bipartisan COPIED Act I introduced with Senator Blackburn and Senator Heinrich, will provide much-needed transparency around AI-generated content. The COPIED Act will also put creators, including local journalists, artists and musicians, back in control of their content with a provenance and watermark process that I think is very much needed.
statements.venue: Press release on COPIED Act introduction

statements.text: OK. My colleague asked about the AI Safety Institute. Will you work with myself and Senator Young and Senator Cruz on an AI Safety Institute that we can get over the goal line that people feel good about?
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for Howard Lutnick as Secretary of Commerce.

statements.text: So now this back again to this big task on export controls and thwarting China and dealing with this AI problem and all the various interests, I mean, I do have some concerns too. [...] And so what do we do about that? What is your solution?
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for Howard Lutnick as Secretary of Commerce, where Senator Cantwell presses the nominee on export controls and illicit finance.

statements.text: But in addition to this AI challenge that we face, the President, in his January 20, 2025, memorandum on America First trade policy, directs you, the Secretary of Commerce, to work with the Secretary of State on the review of those export controls and to advise on modifications in light of developments with strategic adversaries and geopolitical rivals.
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for Howard Lutnick as Secretary of Commerce, where Senator Cantwell outlines the Department's AI-related export-control and semiconductor responsibilities.

statements.text: But now, we are in an innovation race defined by AI and quantum. And according to the World Economic Forum, the U.S. generative AI may increase gross domestic product between $2 and $4 trillion per decade.
statements.context: Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA) speaks on the Senate floor advocating for international collaboration and coalition-building in technology trade, with AI and quantum identified as the defining innovation race.

statements.text: In fact, the administration has already almost abandoned something called the AI Safety Institute, which is widely supported, literally by practicably everybody in the AI sector, and would help us remain a leader. This is the kind of standards that we would expect to be set and the kind of controls that we would hope would help the United States not have some vital technology exported outside the United States.
statements.context: Senate floor speech by Senator Maria Cantwell opposing the nomination of Howard Lutnick as Secretary of Commerce, covering trade, tariffs, CHIPS Act commitments, export controls, and AI governance.

statements.text: Export controls are not a trade strategy. They are not a back pocket issue that the President of the United States whips out in trade negotiations.
statements.context: Senate Commerce Committee hearing on U.S. AI competitiveness where Senator Cantwell delivered opening remarks on compute infrastructure, export controls, and AI standards.

statements.text: We must curb AI's worst excesses while also encouraging growth, which is exactly what states have done through their creation of their own regulatory framework. [...] So clearly, I don't support this part of the legislation, and I appreciate my colleague from Tennessee and her attorney general working on this very important issue.
statements.context: Senate floor speech by Senator Maria Cantwell opposing a provision in a budget reconciliation bill that would preempt state AI regulation, during debate on June 28, 2025.

statements.text: And how do proponents of this moratorium propose to get started? By holding broadband money hostage unless you implement an AI moratorium.
statements.context: Senator Cantwell speaking on the Senate floor against a budget reconciliation bill, criticizing its AI moratorium provision and Medicaid cuts.

statements.text: So, really appreciate the fact that your recommendations call out NIST standards, which is, you know, a bill that Senator Young and I passed out of this committee.
statements.context: Senate committee hearing on the America's AI Action Plan, where Senator Cantwell questions a witness about infrastructure, standards, and export policy.

statements.text: I do not want China to go to the Middle East and capitalize on data centers in the Middle East.
statements.context: Senator Cantwell delivers opening remarks at a Commerce Committee subcommittee hearing on the U.S. AI Action Plan, addressing Director Kratsios.

statements.text: Do you think that we could do a technology NATO kind of alliance with these countries on AI standards or AI innovation?
statements.context: Senator Cantwell poses the question during a panel discussion on America's AI Action Plan.

statements.text: To be clear, I do support a Federal preemption bill, but only when it is paired with the appropriate Federal framework, which includes solid guardrails to ensure that America is the leader in setting AI standards and rules of the road.
statements.context: Senate Commerce Committee confirmation hearing for nominees to the NTSB, OSTP, and Department of Commerce.

statements.text: Well, I think in Senator Blackburn and I's providence model, you would know where the content was created, and you could follow that and demand compensation. In a search AI world, it becomes more opaque as to what information was gathered, and so it becomes even more important, I think, for us to get this right.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on government pressure on Big Tech content moderation, Part II.

statements.text: This executive order’s overly broad preemption threatens states with lawsuits and funding cuts for protecting their residents from AI-powered frauds, scams, and deepfakes—leaving American consumers without any protection. Let’s get it right and pass a bipartisan national AI framework that both leads on innovation and protects consumers.
statements.venue: Statement on Trump AI Executive Order

statements.text: Well, I think we need to be very loud and clear that the Federal Government needs to do something on AI, that you here are telling us the problem with social media but you are basically saying AI is way worse. So it is time to step up.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'Plugged Out: Examining the Impact of Technology on America's Youth,' where Senator Cantwell responds to witness testimony.

statements.text: Well, continuing on the just general questions, I think, Dr. Twenge, your research, you know, pointing to 2012 and the change in policy, do you all believe that Congress should act and do something on AI because the acceleration of those trends are just going to quadruple in problems? Do we need to take action and do something on AI specific?
statements.context: Senate hearing on technology's impact on youth, where Senator Cantwell questions a witness panel on the need for AI legislation.

statements.text: We need meaningful safeguards on AI to address the harms they cause.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'Plugged Out: Examining the Impact of Technology on America's Youth,' where Senator Cantwell delivers opening remarks on social media and AI harms to children.

statements.text: the engagement is being driven by this anger and literally kids are being attacked by agents, by chatbots, the Grok situation. It is like they are purposely being used against children. [...] I brought up all these bills that we need to pass here—the Blackburn bill, the Markey bill—doing something about AI and privacy.
statements.context: Senate hearing on technology's impact on youth, where Senator Cantwell questions witnesses about algorithmic harm and pending privacy legislation.

statements.text: Thank you. And what about this issue related to TikTok where the chatbots are specifically attacking kids on things like eating disorders—some of the Rutgers information? How do we get the word out that this is what is happening? You know, we are doing a good job here evangelizing that we need Federal legislation on AI but what else do we need to do to get parents to realize that TikTok itself and the tools used there are attacking kids?
statements.context: Senate committee hearing on technology's impact on youth, featuring Senator Cantwell questioning witnesses.

statements.text: WISeR is an AI-driven prior authorization program being piloted in six states: Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, and in my home State of Washington. [...] This model inserts a black box computer algorithm into the decisions that should be being made by a physician and the patient. It puts a layer of bureaucracy between seniors and the care their doctors have recommended.
statements.context: Senate floor speech by Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA) during a Medicare executive session, criticizing the CMS WISeR AI-driven prior authorization pilot program.

statements.text: We saw last week with OpenAI’s disclosure of an unprecedented security incident — one of its advanced models broke out of the sandbox and created a complex cyberattack against Hugging Face. AI can design viruses, toxins, biological weapons that can be used to design entirely new pathogens that are difficult to detect and counter. And today’s hearing comes at an important moment as AI accelerates new capabilities that are being unlocked every day.
statements.venue: Senate Commerce hearing on AI and telecommunications networks

statements.text: I think some people are proposing there’s like this self-certification model and we just have to go fast. I think what we have to go fast on is all of us coming together on what are the right security layers to protect our citizens and our nation and to advance our competitiveness.

To manage risks from advanced AI systems we need clear safety standards, continuous testing, and reporting of serious failures. America can lead the world in AI by building systems that are not only more capable, but safer and more secure.
statements.venue: Press release on frontier AI governance framework
